key_insight: In strongly stratified, horizontally sheared flows with no initial vertical shear, turbulence can arise through two distinct routes, but both ultimately generate vertical shear that triggers small-scale Kelvin–Helmholtz mixing at sufficiently high buoyancy Reynolds number.
engineering_relevance: This identifies when nominally horizontal shear in stratified geophysical or industrial flows can still drive diapycnal mixing, helping predict mixing efficiency and vertical transport in high-Re, low-Froude regimes.
method: Linear stability analysis of horizontally sheared stratified flow
Direct numerical simulations to follow nonlinear evolution and secondary instabilities
Comparison of two pathways: vertically modulated primary modes versus columnar vortical evolution
evidence_signal: The abstract reports combined linear theory and DNS showing two instability pathways and their different excited vertical-scale ranges, which produce different peak mixing efficiencies.
watch_item: The results depend on sufficiently large buoyancy Reynolds number, so the mixing pathways and efficiencies may not apply at lower-Re or less strongly stratified conditions.
paper_title: Two pathways to diapycnal mixing in strongly stratified flows with no initial vertical shear
